name: Burnt matchstick lash darkening

card.summary: Burnt matchstick lash darkening is an improvised method of using the charred tip of a match as a homemade mascara to make lashes look darker and fuller.
card.note: Improvised eye products are not tested for eye safety.

quick.overview:
The method uses soot from a burnt match to darken eyelashes, an improvised stand-in for mascara. Darker lashes frame the eyes and make them look larger and more defined, which is the same effect commercial mascara and kohl are used for.

Darkening lashes with soot or ash has a long history: ancient kohl was made from soot and charcoal, and Victorian women made mascara at home from ash or lampblack mixed with elderberry juice.[1] The matchstick version is a folk variant of this idea. No studies have examined it specifically.
quick.how: People describe striking and burning a match, letting it cool, and drawing the charred tip along the lashes. It is described as a short-term, wash-off look.
quick.risks: Homemade eye products are not covered by cosmetic safety testing, and eye-area cosmetics carry known risks of irritation and contamination. A historical lash dye led to blindness and a death in the 1930s and helped lead to US cosmetic regulation.[1]

lead: Burnt matchstick lash darkening is a do-it-yourself way of darkening eyelashes by applying the soot from a burnt match tip, used where mascara is unavailable. It aims at the same look as mascara: lashes that appear darker, denser and longer, with more defined eyes.

It sits in a long tradition of lash darkening. Kohl, used in ancient Egypt from around 4000 BC, was made from materials such as galena, malachite, and charcoal or soot, and Victorian women heated ash or lampblack with elderberry juice to make their own mascara.[1] Commercial mascara followed, including a petroleum jelly and coal product made by Thomas Lyle Williams in 1915 that became Maybelline.[1]
No published trials or safety studies cover the matchstick method itself.

chain: Apply soot from a burnt match to lashes
angle.text: Soot coats the lashes and makes them look darker, as mascara does. The effect lasts until washed off.

paras: The technique takes soot, in this case from a charred match, and applies it to lashes so they look darker. It is an improvisation rather than a product, and is usually described as a stopgap.

Records from about 4000 BC describe kohl in Egypt for darkening lashes, lids and brows, spreading later to Babylonian, Greek and Roman cultures.[1] In the Victorian period women made mascara at home from ash or lampblack and elderberry juice.[1] Eugene Rimmel developed a petroleum jelly cosmetic whose name became a generic word for mascara in several languages, and in 1915 Thomas Lyle Williams made a similar product for his sister, leading to the Maybelline company.[1]

Kohl-type products have posed lead poisoning risks, and in the US they are illegal color additives.[1] The 1933 Lash Lure dye caused blindness in sixteen women and one death from infection, and the case helped prompt the 1938 law giving the FDA authority over cosmetics.[1] Other eye-cosmetic concerns include microbial contamination and irritation.[1]
